subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Find the equation of the parabola whose axis is parallel to the y-axis and passes through the points (4, 5), (−2, 11), (−4, 21).

mark_split.label: Set up the general equation and substitute the three points
Eliminate n to get two equations in l and m
Substitute back for n and write the final equation

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Senior Maths-2B, book p.24 — LAQ chapter 2 Parabola, answer 12 (this scan's page numbering jumps 22 → 24, so the printed page shows both answers 12 and 13; see the ts_ipe_m2b_par_through_points_axis_parallel_x_v1 card for that gap). No appearance year tag is printed next to this question. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS — no margin mark tags are printed anywhere on this page for either answer 12 or 13; the 2/2/2/1 split below follows the same natural break points as the sibling axis-parallel-to-x-axis question (answer 10 / Bullet MP Q20), since both are the identical method with x and y exchanged. No two-book union check was possible for Maths-2B (no second-year TSBIE Basic Learning Material is on hand), and no board back-test beyond diffing against this book's own five Guess Papers.

steps.label: Set up the general equation
steps.margin_note: First two marks, for the correct general form and all three substitutions.
lines: The equation of a parabola with axis parallel to the y-axis is y = lx² + mx + n.
steps.why: An axis parallel to the y-axis means y is written in terms of x², the familiar shape of an upward or downward parabola — three unknowns need three points, exactly as given.
common_mistakes: Writing the general form as x = ly² + my + n, the axis-parallel-to-x-axis case instead.
Sign-slipping on the negative x-coordinates when squaring them.
steps.memory_tip: Axis along y means y is written in terms of x — y = lx² + mx + n, the everyday shape from school.

steps.label: Eliminate n
steps.margin_note: Two marks. The m-coefficients look small but the sign changes are where marks are usually lost.
steps.why: Subtracting equation (2) from each of the other two removes n immediately, and leaves a pair of equations in only l and m.
common_mistakes: Subtracting (2) from (1) but computing the m-terms as 4m − (−2m) = 2m instead of the correct 6m.
Dropping the factor of 12 shared by both new equations before combining them.
steps.memory_tip: Subtract the middle equation from the other two — n cancels both times, leaving a clean 2×2 system in l and m.

steps.label: Solve for m and l
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Both unknowns fall out cleanly here because the coefficients of l happen to match.
steps.why: Subtracting (5) from (4) cancels the l-terms this time, since both carry the same 12l, and that hands over m directly; l then follows from a one-line substitution.
common_mistakes: Adding (4) and (5) instead of subtracting, which leaves l in the equation rather than cancelling it.
Forgetting to substitute the value of m back into (4) and instead guessing l.
steps.memory_tip: This time it is l, not n, that shares the same coefficient in both new equations — subtract to cancel it and read off m.

steps.label: Write the final equation
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Check the boxed equation by substituting (4, 5) back in — it should give 0.
lines: Substitute l = 1/2, m = −2, n = 5 in y = lx² + mx + n:
steps.why: Multiplying by 2 clears the only fraction in the equation and leaves the standard whole-number form for a locus.
common_mistakes: Leaving the final equation with the 1/2 fraction still in it instead of clearing it.
Writing the boxed line as x² − 2y − 4x + 10 = 0 without checking it is the same equation, just reordered — both forms are correct, but a term must not be dropped while rearranging.
steps.memory_tip: Multiply through by 2 the moment a fraction appears — one clean whole-number equation is the target.

insider_note: The book reaches n by putting l and m back into equation (1); putting them into (2) or (3) instead gives the same n and is a fast, free check most students skip.
